title: Navigating the biopsychosocial landscape: A systematic review on the association between social support and chronic pain
authors: Carlo Matej Rinaudo; Maxim Van de Velde; Arnaud Steyaert; André Mouraux; Bianka Karshikoff
pain_condition_detail: unspecified chronic pain conditions, musculoskeletal pain, fibromyalgia, spinal cord injury, neurological/neuromuscular pain or disability, chronic migraine/headache, post-surgical pain (breast surgery), chronic pelvic pain, articular pain
context_note: Studies mainly conducted in USA, Canada or Europe; only three studies from South Korea and Australia.
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS model as background framing to justify studying social support in chronic pain. It does not operationalize the model; it focuses exclusively on social support (a social factor) and its associations with psychological and pain outcomes, with no biological content.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper reports associations between social support constructs and psychological/pain outcomes but does not specify pathways or mechanisms linking domains.
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies
quality_assessment_tools_2: hawker et al. quality assessment tool
emergent_labels_10: Informal Social Support for Autonomy and Dependence in Pain Inventory
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper invokes the BPS model but contains no biological content, creating a tension between the label and the actual scope
conceptual_tensions_2: Social support is conceptualized as both a protective factor (PSS, SSS) and a risk factor (SpR), but the mechanisms for this duality are not explored
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper notes that PSS and SSS are related but distinct constructs, yet does not clarify how they interact or whether they should be studied together
additional_observations_1: The paper provides a detailed operationalization of social support constructs (PSS, SSS, SpR) with definitions and examples, which is a strength for the social domain
additional_observations_2: The review uses vote counting based on direction of effect due to heterogeneity, which limits the strength of conclusions
additional_observations_3: The paper recommends using the SRI for future studies on spousal responses, showing attention to measurement specificity
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes the BPS model narrowly by focusing on social support and its associations with psychological outcomes, with no biological content. It provides a detailed conceptualization of social support constructs but does not integrate domains mechanistically. The BPS label serves as background framing rather than an analytic framework.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but biology is absent. Triadic integration is none due to missing biological domain. Social and psychological domains are descriptively associated but not mechanistically linked.

title: Navigating the biopsychosocial landscape: A systematic review on the association between social support and chronic pain
authors: Carlo Matej Rinaudo; Maxim Van de Velde; Arnaud Steyaert; André Mouraux; Bianka Karshikoff
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (persistent or recurrent pain lasting longer than 3 months), including musculoskeletal pain, fibromyalgia, spinal cord injury, neurological/neuromuscular pain or disability, chronic migraine/headache, post-surgical pain, chronic pelvic pain, articular pain, and unspecified chronic pain.
context_note: Studies were mainly conducted in the USA, Canada or Europe; only three studies were outside these regions (South Korea and Australia); authors note Western-country generalisability limits.
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS mainly to justify a social-support focus, then operationalizes only social support (PSS, SSS, SpR) and compares them with pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety outcomes. It does not code or model biological, psychological, and social domains as an integrated system.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a social-support pathway in which support buffers stress through stress appraisal and active coping, potentially reducing pain; spousal responses may reinforce pain behaviour through operant learning. It does not specify a full three-domain mechanism in which biological, psychological, and social factors reciprocally shape one another.
quality_assessment_tools_1: adapted version of the “jbi critical appraisal checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies”
quality_assessment_tools_3: adapted version of the quality assessment tool of hawker et al
emergent_labels_11: operant conditioning theory of chronic pain
conceptual_tensions_1: The BPS label frames chronic pain as biological, psychological, and social, but the review’s operational exposure is social support rather than all three domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Social support generally appears beneficial, but spousal responses can be associated with worse pain, disability, and depression
conceptual_tensions_3: The evidence base is mostly cross-sectional and correlational, yet the paper discusses possible causality and future longitudinal designs
conceptual_tensions_4: Different social support constructs and questionnaires create inconsistency and obscure whether PSS, SSS, and SpR have comparable meanings
conceptual_tensions_5: Spousal responses are explicitly not a measure of social support per se, yet they are included as an important chronic-pain social factor
additional_observations_1: The review does not perform meta-analysis, it uses vote counting and correlation/regression direction because of heterogeneity and lack of effect sizes
additional_observations_2: No included studies were randomized, and only eight of 40 final studies were longitudinal
additional_observations_3: Spousal responses are treated as a social exposure because they influence pain behaviour and well-being, even though the paper says they are not social support per se
additional_observations_4: The paper’s closest triadic mechanism is stress-buffering through stress appraisal and active coping, but it is not tied to a full BPS operational model
additional_observations_5: Biological content is concentrated in pain/nociception definitions and pain outcomes rather than mechanisms such as inflammation, genetics, imaging, or peripheral sensitization
additional_observations_6: The conclusion recommends spouse education and including spouses in treatment sessions, which turns social support findings into applied pain-management suggestions
synthesis_note: This review uses a BPS-labeled title/intro but operationalizes social support rather than the full BPS model. It codes PSS, SSS, and SpR against pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety, mostly with cross-sectional correlations. It offers stress-buffering and operant-learning pathways but no full biological-psychological-social system.
coding_rationale: Social support dominates; psychological outcomes are developed; biological content is limited to pain/nociception. BPS frames the topic but does not create a triadic mechanism, so pseudo_bps/partial integration.

title: Navigating the biopsychosocial landscape: A systematic review on the association between social support and chronic pain
authors: Carlo Matej Rinaudo; Maxim Van de Velde; Arnaud Steyaert; André Mouraux; Bianka Karshikoff
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain conditions including musculoskeletal, fibromyalgia, spinal cord injury, migraine, post-surgical, pelvic pain, and articular pain.
context_note: Studies conducted mainly in USA, Canada, Europe; limited representation from South Korea and Australia.
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes the review around social support constructs (PSS, SSS, SpR) within a BPS framework, but focuses exclusively on social domain with psychological outcomes; biological domain absent.
integration_mechanism_summary: Directional associations from social factors to psychological outcomes: higher perceived social support and satisfaction associated with lower depression and higher mental QoL; spousal responses positively associated with pain intensity and depression. No biological domain integration proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS theoretical framework requiring biological integration and the review's exclusive focus on social-psychological associations
conceptual_tensions_2: Contradictory findings for PSS effects on pain intensity: some studies show negative associations while others show positive or no associations
conceptual_tensions_3: Ambiguity in interpreting spousal responses: beneficial support vs. potentially reinforcing pain behaviors
additional_observations_1: Review focuses exclusively on social support constructs without any biological mechanisms or measures
additional_observations_2: Operant conditioning theory used to explain spousal response effects on pain behaviors
additional_observations_3: Stress-buffering model referenced as theoretical framework for social support effects
additional_observations_4: High heterogeneity in measurement instruments across studies limits synthesis
additional_observations_5: Predominantly cross-sectional design prevents causal inference
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes the BPS label as an organizing framework for studying social support in chronic pain, but provides no substantive biological content. The review examines three social support constructs (perceived, satisfaction, spousal responses) and their associations with psychological outcomes like depression and anxiety. While directional social-psychological associations are identified, the biological domain is entirely absent, representing a pseudo-BPS approach that uses the label without three-domain integration.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial (social-psychological focus) with no biological integration. Social domain is elaborated, psychological domain elaborated, biological absent. Integration is directional between social and psychological domains only.
